title: Politics in India: Era of One-Party Dominance

topics.title: The challenge of building democracy: the first general election

learn.hook: In 1951-52 about 17 crore Indians, most of whom could not read, were invited to choose their government. Many observers abroad expected the experiment to fail. It did not.
points: India chose democracy with universal adult franchise from the start: every adult citizen got the right to vote, regardless of literacy, wealth, caste or gender. Many countries had given this right only gradually.
The Election Commission of India was set up in January 1950, and Sukumar Sen became the first Chief Election Commissioner.

The first general election was a huge exercise: about 17 crore voters, most of them not literate, electing about 489 members of the Lok Sabha and members of state assemblies. It was postponed twice and finally held from October 1951 to February 1952.

Voting methods have changed: in the first two elections each candidate had a separate ballot box marked with a symbol, and voters dropped their ballot paper into the box of their choice. Later, ballot papers listed names and symbols, and from the late 1990s Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) were introduced; by 2004 the whole country used EVMs.
The success of the first election proved that democracy could work even in a poor and largely non-literate country.

example.q: Why were symbols important in India's first general election?
steps: Most voters were not literate and could not read candidates' names.
Each candidate had a ballot box marked with a symbol.
Voters could recognise the symbol and cast their vote.
example.answer: Because most voters could not read, symbols helped them identify candidates

learn.reallife: Today's EVMs and VVPATs, used in elections from Ladakh to Lakshadweep, grew out of the Election Commission's long effort to make voting simpler and faster.

topics.title: Congress dominance in the first three general elections

learn.hook: In 1952 one party won about three out of every four seats in the Lok Sabha, yet less than half the votes. The secret lies in the voting system.
points: The Congress won the first three general elections (1952, 1957 and 1962) by large margins and also formed governments in almost all states.
In 1952 the Congress won 364 of the 489 Lok Sabha seats. The Communist Party of India came second with only 16 seats.

India uses the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system: the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins, even without a majority. Because opposition votes were split among many parties, the Congress won about three-fourths of the seats with less than half of the votes.

An exception came in Kerala in 1957, where the Communist Party of India won the assembly election and formed a government under E.M.S. Namboodiripad. The central government dismissed it in 1959 under Article 356.

example.q: In a constituency, Congress gets 40% votes, Party B 35% and Party C 25%. Who wins under FPTP, and why does this matter?
steps: Under FPTP, the candidate with the most votes wins.
Congress has the most votes (40%), so it wins, even though 60% voted against it.
Repeated across many constituencies, this gives a seat share much bigger than the vote share.
example.answer: Congress wins; FPTP can turn a minority of votes into a large share of seats

learn.reallife: A batsman who scores the most runs wins 'man of the match' even if he did not score half the team's runs. FPTP rewards the top scorer in each seat the same way.

topics.title: Nature of Congress dominance: a social and ideological coalition

learn.hook: One party, many voices: socialists and conservatives, farmers and industrialists, villagers and city folk, all under one roof.
points: One-party dominance existed in other countries too, but often without democracy. For example, the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) ruled Mexico for about sixty years under conditions that were not fully democratic. In India, Congress dominance happened under free and fair, democratic elections.
Its roots lay in the legacy of the national movement: the Congress was seen as the inheritor of the freedom struggle, and it had the widest organisation, reaching almost every village.
The Congress was a social coalition: it brought together peasants and industrialists, urban and rural people, workers and owners, the middle, lower and upper classes and castes.
It was also an ideological coalition: it accommodated revolutionaries and pacifists, conservatives and radicals, extremists and moderates, and those on the right, left and centre.

example.q: How was Congress dominance in India different from the PRI's dominance in Mexico?
steps: The PRI ruled Mexico for decades under conditions that were not fully democratic.
The Congress won repeatedly in free and fair elections with many opposition parties.
So Indian one-party dominance existed within democracy.
example.answer: Congress dominance was achieved democratically; the PRI's was not

learn.reallife: A big joint family where cousins disagree but still sit at one table is a good picture of the Congress as a coalition of many groups.

learn.hook: In the early years, some of the sharpest criticism of the Congress came from inside the Congress itself.
points: Groups within a party are called factions. The Congress had many factions based on ideology or personal ambition and rivalries.
Instead of being a weakness, factions became a strength: they acted as an internal opposition, criticising leaders and policies from within, and forcing the party to adjust.

The coalition-like nature of the Congress encouraged tolerance of differences. Even a faction that was unhappy with the leadership usually stayed inside the party and tried to change it, rather than leaving.
Because of this, the Congress could accommodate many interests, and opposition parties found it hard to grow, since many of their concerns were already voiced by groups within the Congress.

example.q: Why did unhappy groups often stay within the Congress rather than leave?
steps: The party tolerated differences and had a coalition character.
Factions could influence policies from within.
Leaving would mean losing access to the dominant party's organisation and power.
example.answer: Because the party tolerated factions, giving them a voice inside

learn.reallife: In a cricket team, players may argue about batting order but still play for the same side. Congress factions behaved much the same way.

topics.title: Opposition parties: the Socialists and the Communists

learn.hook: Some of India's earliest opposition leaders had sat in Congress meetings for years before walking out to build their own parties.
points: The Congress Socialist Party was formed within the Congress in 1934 by young leaders who wanted a more radical, egalitarian Congress. In 1948 the Congress barred dual membership, so the socialists left and formed the Socialist Party.

Leaders of the socialists included Acharya Narendra Dev, Ram Manohar Lohia and Jayaprakash Narayan. They believed in democratic socialism and criticised the Congress for favouring capitalists and landlords. The party later went through many splits and mergers.
Communist groups emerged in the early 1920s, inspired by the Bolshevik revolution in Russia. The Communist Party of India (CPI) worked with the Congress for some years before separating.

CPI leaders included A.K. Gopalan, S.A. Dange, E.M.S. Namboodiripad, P.C. Joshi, Ajay Ghosh and P. Sundarraya. In 1952 the CPI won 16 seats and was the largest opposition party. It split in 1964, and the CPI(M) was formed.

example.q: Classify these leaders as Socialist or Communist: Ram Manohar Lohia, A.K. Gopalan, Jayaprakash Narayan, S.A. Dange.
steps: Lohia: Socialist.
Gopalan: Communist.
Jayaprakash Narayan: Socialist.
Dange: Communist.
example.answer: Socialist: Lohia, JP; Communist: Gopalan, Dange

learn.reallife: Many trade unions and farmers' groups in Kerala and West Bengal trace their history to the communist movement, while socialist ideas shaped later parties across north India.

topics.title: Bharatiya Jana Sangh, Swatantra Party and the role of the opposition

learn.hook: Nehru's first cabinet included leaders who would later found or lead rival parties. Early Indian democracy valued a strong opposition voice.
points: The Bharatiya Jana Sangh was formed in 1951, with Syama Prasad Mookerjee as its founder-president. It emphasised the idea of one country, one culture and one nation, believing the country could become modern and strong on the basis of Indian culture and traditions. It favoured Hindi as the official language. Leaders included Deen Dayal Upadhyaya and Balraj Madhok. It is the precursor of the Bharatiya Janata Party.

The Swatantra Party was formed in August 1959 after the Congress's Nagpur resolution called for land ceilings, state trading in food grains and cooperative farming. Its leaders included C. Rajagopalachari, K.M. Munshi, N.G. Ranga and Minoo Masani.
The Swatantra Party favoured a free-market economy and less government control. It opposed central planning, nationalisation and the licence system, and favoured closer ties with the USA.

Although they won few seats, opposition parties played a crucial role: they offered principled criticism of Congress policies, kept the ruling party accountable and prevented resentment from becoming anti-democratic.

Early leaders respected the opposition: Nehru's first cabinet after independence (before the first general election) included non-Congress figures like B.R. Ambedkar and Syama Prasad Mookerjee. Exercise tip: match parties with their leaders and explain Congress dominance.

example.q: Match each party with its founding leader: Bharatiya Jana Sangh, Swatantra Party, Socialist Party.
steps: Bharatiya Jana Sangh: Syama Prasad Mookerjee (1951).
Swatantra Party: C. Rajagopalachari (1959).
Socialist Party: Acharya Narendra Dev, among others.
example.answer: BJS - Mookerjee; Swatantra - Rajagopalachari; Socialist - Narendra Dev

learn.reallife: Parliament's Question Hour, when opposition members question ministers, continues the tradition of accountability that early opposition parties built.
